---
title: "Migrating from renv to rig"
toc-depth: 3
---

You already use renv to keep an R project's packages reproducible.
What would change if rig managed the project instead?

This tutorial compares how the two tools manage dependencies and what working with a rig project looks like in Positron or RStudio.
If you decide to switch, the migration steps walk you through importing your dependencies, preserving the environment your analysis needs, and checking the result in your editor.
You keep working in your editor; the change is how you declare, install, and share the project's dependencies.

You need a working renv project, a backup of that project, and rig installed with the `rig proj renv import` command available.
See [Installing rig](install.qmd) if you need to install it.
Run terminal commands from the project's root directory; run R examples in an R session opened in that same directory.
The terminal commands work in both a Unix shell and PowerShell.

::: callout-warning
## Experimental, and not an exact lock-file conversion

`rig proj` is experimental: its commands and file formats may change.
Importing `renv.lock` is a starting point, not a guarantee of an identical environment.
rig imports package names and version requirements, but not their repository or remote-source information.
Keep your backup until you have checked the rig environment and run your project's analysis or tests.

If you only want rig to manage R installations, you can keep using renv for packages.
You do not need to migrate to `rig proj` to use rig.
:::

## How rig projects differ from renv

Both tools give a project its own package library and a lock file to share with collaborators.
In `renv.lock`, package names, exact versions, and source information are recorded together.
rig separates the requirements from their resolution:

- **`rproj.toml`** is the human-facing manifest. It declares the packages the project needs, with version requirements and any source constraints.
- **`rproj.lock`** records the resolved environment: exact versions, download locations, and the dependency graph, including packages needed by other packages.

You can read and edit the project's requirements without working through all the installation details.
Those details remain available in the lock file when you need to inspect them, but rig maintains that file for you.

The commands reflect that separation:

| Task | renv | `rig proj` |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Record dependencies | `renv::snapshot()` records packages from the library according to the project's snapshot settings. | `rproj.toml` declares requirements; `rig proj lock` resolves them into `rproj.lock`. |
| Add a dependency | Install it, then snapshot. | `rig proj add` updates the manifest, lock file, and library. |
| Recreate the environment | `renv::restore()` installs packages from `renv.lock`. | `rig proj sync` installs packages from `rproj.lock` and installs the locked R version if needed. |
| Manage R itself | Records the R version, but does not install R. | Manages R installations as well as package dependencies. |
| Work in an editor | renv's `.Rprofile` auto-loader configures the library. | rig's `.Renviron` and `.rvenvlib` configure the library; the editor still needs to select the appropriate R executable. |

With renv, snapshotting records the relevant state of an installed library.
With rig, the declared requirements are the input, and the installed library is built from the resolved lock file.
Installing a package in the R console does not add it to rig's declarations.

For the everyday experience in Positron or RStudio, skip to [Working with a rig project](#working-with-a-rig-project).
To make the switch, follow the migration steps below.

## Migration steps

### 1. Save a working renv baseline

Make a backup of the project directory before changing either tool's configuration.
Include hidden files and the existing `renv/` directory, not only files tracked by Git.
Continue working in your original project directory for the rest of this tutorial; the backup is there if you need to undo the migration.

In your project's **renv-enabled R session**, check whether the code, installed library, and lock file agree.
The [renv status reference](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/reference/status.html) explains how to interpret any differences.

``` r
renv::status()
```

If renv reports differences, decide which state you want to preserve.
If the installed packages are the ones your working analysis needs, record them with `renv::snapshot()`:

``` r
renv::snapshot()
```

Review the proposed changes before accepting them.
Snapshotting uses your project's configured snapshot type; it does not necessarily record every installed package.
If the lock file instead represents the known-good state, use `renv::restore()` to restore it before migrating.

Run your analysis or tests in this renv environment and save the results you will compare later.
Keep the baseline lock file in version control as well as in your backup.

### 2. Turn off renv's startup activation

Deactivate renv **before importing the project**, while you still have an R session using the renv library:

``` r
renv::deactivate(clean = FALSE)
```

This removes renv's auto-loader from the project `.Rprofile`, but retains `renv.lock` and the project library.
renv restarts the session; close that session before continuing in the terminal.

The distinction matters because rig's import does not deactivate renv.
If `.Rprofile` still sources `renv/activate.R`, starting R can reactivate the old library even after you have created a rig environment.
Inspect `.Rprofile` for any custom renv activation code, preserving unrelated startup settings.
Do not use `clean = TRUE` here: it deletes the lock file and `renv/` directory you are keeping for comparison and rollback.
See [renv's activation reference](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/reference/activate.html).

### 3. Import and inspect the manifest

In the terminal, import the saved lock file:

``` sh
rig proj renv import
```

The import reads `renv.lock` and creates a **manifest**, `rproj.toml`: a file that declares what the project needs.
It also adds rig's startup settings to `.Renviron`, creates `.rvenvlib/rvenv`, and adds `.rvenv` to `.gitignore`.
Existing `.Renviron` and `.gitignore` content is preserved outside rig's managed blocks.
No packages are installed yet, and `renv.lock` is left alone.

Open `rproj.toml` before running any more commands.
For example, a lock file recording R 4.5.2 and cli 3.6.5 produces these requirements:

``` toml
[dependencies]
R = ">= 4.5"
cli = "^3.6.5"
```

This is an excerpt, not a manifest to paste over your imported file.
Your manifest also has project metadata and an entry for each package in your lock file, including transitive dependencies: packages needed by other packages.

#### Keep the first migration separate from an upgrade

The imported requirements allow version changes.
`R = ">= 4.5"` allows newer R versions, and `cli = "^3.6.5"` allows cli versions from 3.6.5 up to, but not including, 4.0.0.
A caret requirement is not an exact pin.

For a first migration, edit the imported requirements to match the versions in your baseline lock file.
For the example above, change the requirements to:

``` toml
[dependencies]
R = "= 4.5.2"
cli = "= 3.6.5"
```

The leading `=` requests that exact version.
Apply the same change to the other repository packages you want to preserve, not only packages you call directly.
Removing the caret without adding `=` does **not** pin a package: a bare version such as `"3.6.5"` also means a compatible-version range.

Exact requirements prevent the solver from silently choosing newer versions; they do not recover package sources that the import discarded.
A version that is unavailable for a chosen target may still prevent locking or installation.

#### Restore package sources that import does not carry over

Compare the imported entries with the `Source`, `Repository`, and `Remote*` fields in `renv.lock`.
The import uses package names and versions, not those source fields.
Review these cases before locking:

- **GitHub or other Git packages:** replace the imported version-only entry with a Git dependency, retaining the original commit when you need the same code. The [dependency reference](reference/proj.qmd#rig-proj-add) describes Git dependencies and revision syntax.
- **Private or other CRAN-like repositories:** add the repository to `rproj.toml` and pin the relevant packages to it. See [project repositories](reference/proj.qmd#repositories). rig does not inherit repositories from your R session or `renv.lock`.
- **Local packages and package archives:** declare the appropriate path or URL dependency using the [dependency reference](reference/proj.qmd#rig-proj-add). Check that collaborators can access the same source.
- **Bioconductor packages:** check the intended release as well as package versions. rig's default release follows the chosen R version; see [the lock reference](reference/proj.qmd#rig-proj-lock) for how to select a release explicitly.

renv profiles and Python environment metadata are not imported either.
If your project depends on them, plan their replacement separately before switching.

::: callout-note
## If the import refuses to proceed

If rig reports `rproj.toml already exists`, stop and check whether this directory is already a rig project.
`rig proj renv import --dependencies` merges dependencies into an existing manifest, overwriting matching dependency entries; it is not a fresh migration and does not create the full startup setup.

If rig reports conflicting startup files, inspect them rather than immediately passing `--force`.
That flag permits replacement of rig's generated files.
:::

### 4. Resolve and install the rig environment

Once the manifest describes the versions and sources you want, resolve it:

``` sh
rig proj lock
```

This creates `rproj.lock`, rig's **lock file**: the exact package versions and download locations for each resolved R-version/platform target.
Unlike renv's snapshot, locking solves the requirements in a manifest; it does not inspect the packages in your old library.
Review `rproj.lock` against your baseline before installing anything.
See [R projects](proj-guide.qmd#platforms-and-r-versions) for choosing the platforms to lock for.

Preview the installation from that lock file:

``` sh
rig proj sync --dry-run
```

The preview shows what sync would install or write without changing the R installation or project environment.
If locking fails or the preview names an unexpected package version, return to the manifest.
Check exact constraints, package sources, repository access, and target platforms rather than relaxing constraints only to make the error disappear.

When you are satisfied with the plan, install from the reviewed lock file:

``` sh
rig proj sync --locked
```

`--locked` requires a lock file consistent with the manifest.
Sync installs packages into `.rvenv/lib` by default and writes R wrappers under `.rvenv/bin`; it does not copy your renv library.
It also installs the locked R version if that version is missing.

This works in both [admin mode and user mode](admin-vs-user-mode.qmd).
The mode determines where R is installed and whether that installation needs elevated privileges; it does not change the manifest-and-lock workflow.
Source packages may need compilers or system libraries.
On Linux, installing missing system packages can need administrator rights even in user mode; see [the `rig proj sync` system requirements](reference/proj.qmd#system-requirements).

### 5. Check the project in Positron or RStudio

Open your project folder in Positron, or reopen your existing project in RStudio.
Start a fresh R session.

The project's `.Renviron` and `.rvenvlib` configure the package library when R starts.
You do not need to run `rig run` or activate a shell to use the project in your editor.
However, rig's startup files do not choose which R executable the editor starts.
In the R console, check the running R version and library search paths:

``` r
getRversion()
.libPaths()
```

Check that the R version matches your lock file and that the project library is present.
With the default layout, that library is `.rvenv/lib`, not `renv/library`.
Other libraries, including rig's tools library and R's base library, can also appear; the paths are not expected to contain only one entry.

If R still uses the renv library, revisit `.Rprofile` and check for custom renv activation.
If the R version is wrong, change the editor's R selection.
Restart R after either change; an already-running session keeps its library configuration.
Opening the project does not run `rig proj sync` automatically: we installed the environment explicitly in step 4.

Now run the same analysis or tests you used for the renv baseline, using your editor as usual.
Compare results, not only whether packages load.
Matching version numbers alone cannot prove that the project behaves identically: package sources, system libraries, and external tools also matter.

::: callout-note
## Optional terminal check

To check the environment independently of your editor's R selection, run `rig run` from the project directory.
It starts R through the project's wrapper, using the project's R version and library.
Run `getRversion()` and `.libPaths()` there to compare with your editor session.
This is also useful for running scripts from a terminal, but it is not a required step when opening the editor.
:::

## Working with a rig project {#working-with-a-rig-project}

Keep editing scripts, loading packages, running analyses, and rendering documents in Positron or RStudio as before.
The main change is how you manage dependencies: use rig in your editor's **Terminal** pane, rather than installing packages in the R console and snapshotting afterward.
Run these terminal commands from the project root.

For example, if your project needs dplyr, declare it with:

``` sh
rig proj add dplyr
```

This updates the manifest, locks dependencies, and syncs the project library.
Return to the R console and use `library(dplyr)` as usual.
If the operation replaced a package already loaded in your session, restart R before using its new version.
You no longer need a separate `renv::snapshot()` step.

Calling `install.packages()` in R does not update `rproj.toml` or `rproj.lock`.
Declare project dependencies with `rig proj add` so collaborators can recreate them, rather than relying on packages installed only on your machine.

Commit `rproj.toml`, `rproj.lock`, `.rvenvlib`, the `.gitignore` update, and the startup-file changes.
Review `.Renviron` before committing it: rig's boilerplate belongs in version control, but any credentials or machine-specific settings already in that file do not.
Do not commit `.rvenv`; each machine rebuilds its own environment.

After pulling dependency changes from a collaborator, or cloning the project on another machine, install the committed environment from the Terminal pane:

``` sh
rig proj sync --locked
```

This brings the local environment into line with the lock file.
Restart your R session if packages changed, and select the project's R version if it changed too.
You can use `rig proj status` to check the manifest, lock file, and local environment's status.

Update project setup instructions and continuous integration (CI) scripts to use `rig proj sync --locked` rather than `renv::restore()`.
Check that CI has rig installed, can reach the required package sources, and runs the same tests.
Test a fresh checkout before asking collaborators to switch.

Keep `renv.lock` and `renv/` until the migration has been checked by everyone who needs it.
After that, remove the unused renv files and any remaining renv setup calls deliberately.
Do not delete renv's global cache to clean up one project: other renv projects may still use it.

## If you need to go back

Close the R session and save any work you have done since making the backup.
Replace the migrated project directory with the backed-up directory, then reopen the project in your editor with its original R version.
The backup retains the original startup files, lock file, and renv library; use `renv::restore()` if you need to restore packages.

Restore the whole project setup, not only `renv.lock`: rig's `.Renviron` settings would otherwise still configure the library.

## Where to next

You now have a declared set of dependencies, a reviewed rig lock file, and a project library tested against your renv baseline.
Keep the first successful migration as a checkpoint before loosening version requirements or upgrading packages.

- [R projects](proj-guide.qmd): dependency groups, multiple platforms, and named project scripts.
- [The `rig proj` reference](reference/proj.qmd): the full command and option reference.
- [The renv introduction](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html): background on renv libraries, lock files, and deactivation.
